title: The complexity standard is not a skill
statement: Tag a reading item with the operation it actually demands, never with the text-complexity standard as if that band were the skill tested.
example: A live audit of 40 Grade 5 items found the genre tag right on all 40 but the subskill defensible on only 34.
detail: A live audit of a Grade 5 reading course's items found genre tagging strong and subskill tagging weaker: 40 of 40 genre tags matched, but only 34 of 40 subskills were defensible, with the text-complexity band (the standard numbered .10) used as a skill and two items miscoded on another standard. The course's acceptance criteria call for recoding those items and auditing enough final items to show the tags match the cognitive work, and its retrospective records the standards and subskill clean-up as only partial.

evidence.quote: D8 live audit found 40/40 genre match but only 34/40 subskill defensible, with `.10` text-complexity band used as a skill and two RL.5.6 miscoded items. | Recode `.10` and wrong subskill items; audit enough final items to prove cognitive-work alignment. |
Standards/subskill cleanup was partial. A D8 sample found strong genre tagging but weaker subskill precision, especially where text-complexity bands and standard codes were being used loosely.
